text: 51-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with persistent, forceful vomiting after consuming a significant amount of alcohol. His medical history includes recent treatment for Lyme disease with doxycycline. Recently, after a prolonged episode of retching, the patient starts to choke and cough forcefully, experiencing chest pain. The patient appears unable to communicate effectively at this point.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the history of forceful vomiting followed by sudden chest pain and difficulty breathing, I suspect a Boerhaave syndrome (esophageal rupture). REQUEST TEST: Chest_X-Ray. REQUEST TEST: CT_Chest_with_contrast.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Chest_X-ray: Free mediastinal air visible, suggesting perforation. CT_Chest_with_contrast: NORMAL READINGS

speaker: Doctor
text:
The presence of free mediastinal air on the chest X-ray is highly specific for esophageal perforation, even if the CT scan was initially read as normal, which can happen in early or subtle cases. Given the classic presentation of forceful vomiting followed by chest pain and pneumomediastinum, I am confident in the clinical picture.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Boerhaave syndrome (esophageal rupture)
